title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
question: Can a large frozen pretrained model be adapted to downstream tasks by training a low-rank additive update, avoiding full fine-tuning cost and adapter inference latency?
mechanism: For frozen W0, the layer computes h = W0 x + dW x = W0 x + B A x, with B (d x r) zero-initialized and A Gaussian-initialized; dW x is scaled by alpha/r, and alpha is set once rather than tuned. Only A and B are trained. After training, W = W0 + BA is stored or merged, so inference uses the original architecture.
training: Gradient training (Adam) of A and B only, on each task's conditional language-modelling objective over (x,y) pairs; W0 is frozen. Dataset sizes are in the experiment sections, which were not recovered.
inference_cost: Zero added latency once merged (paper claim). Unmerged adapter layers add latency: Table 1 (GPT-2 medium, ms) gives Fine-Tune/LoRA 1449.4, 338.0, 19.8 with AdapterL +2.2%, +5.0%, +20.7% and AdapterH +3.0%, +8.4%, +30.3% at batch 32, 16, 1.
setup: GPT-3 175B (headline case); RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2; NLG tasks summarization, MRC and NL2SQL (Sec. 2). Latency study on GPT-2 medium.
numbers: LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times (Abstract).
the amplification factor is rather huge: 21.5 ≈ 6.91/0.32 for r = 4 (Sec. 7, after Table 7).
limits: Authors say the mechanism behind fine-tuning or LoRA 'is far from clear' (Sec. 8). Prefix tuning is non-monotone in trainable parameters and shortens usable sequence length (Sec. 3).
evidence_quote: Our simple linear design allows us to merge the trainable matrices with the frozen weights when deployed, introducing no inference latency compared to a fully fine-tuned model, by construction.

title: Symbolic Synthesis of Neural Networks
question: Do neural modules whose inputs are modified by synthesized symbolic-program features improve data efficiency and generalization on a binary high-dimensional task?
mechanism: A G-SSNN is m(x) = m_gnn(graph_mape(g, x)). A symbolic program produces a graph g of local, discrete features; a static embedding function e transforms regions of the input vector per feature; a GINE graph network then processes the result. Programs are evolved with library learning (STITCH) and heap search, and the population is pruned by rank-LTP-50, which discards the bottom half by training performance at each step.
training: Standard gradient training of each G-SSNN's GNN, inside an outer evolutionary loop that selects programs. Trained on a binary Raven's Progressive Matrices task with 'small quantities of data' (Abstract); exact sample counts were not recovered.
setup: Binary prediction over Raven's Progressive Matrices (RPMs). Baseline: a ViT-style model with convolutional stem (2 blocks, 128-d heads). Experimental: GINE with 512-d node and edge features, three layers.
numbers: Among baseline models less than 20% fall in this range. (Sec. 5.3; range = validation accuracy highest at 80-90% training accuracy)
After the first iteration, 30% or more of the population of experimental models fall in this range. (Sec. 5.3)
by the third iteration 20% or more of experimental models fall in this range (Sec. 5.3).
limits: Single population, single task (Sec. 3). The conclusion defers investigation of data efficiency and transfer to more complex symbolic programs. No final accuracy table is in the read text.
evidence_quote: The symbolic program is chosen by an evolutionary algorithm, which is used to develop and evaluate a population of G-SSNNs with varying designs.

title: Decouple knowledge from parameters for plug-and-play language modeling
question: Can a pretrained language model decouple knowledge from its FFN parameters by using an editable plug-in key-value memory, so knowledge can be added or updated without retraining?
mechanism: FFN layers in the top L transformer layers are replaced by a differentiable plug-in key-value memory DPM = <D, K, V>. Each knowledge segment d_n is encoded by attention pooling to h_n; keys are k_n = W_k h_n + b_k and values v_n = W_v h_n + v_k. Hidden states retrieve knowledge by maximum inner product search over K and combine it through knowledge attention (Sec. 4.2; the exact combination formula was not recovered). The paper claims entries can be updated in a training-free way.
training: Pretraining with the DPM on unlabeled corpora, then fine-tuning stages (Sec. 4.3; details not recovered). Knowledge update is claimed to be training-free, meaning an edit to DPM entries after pretraining.
inference_cost: Table 1 reports 'Avg. Cost' as adaptation time in hours; for PlugLM this is the time to encode domain knowledge into the knowledge base, not per-query cost. Per-query inference cost not recovered.
setup: BERT-base architecture; domain adaptation over four domains; knowledge update on LINNAEUS NER; SQuAD (Table 2); biomedical NER over eight datasets (Table 3).
numbers: 3.95 F1 improvements across four domains on average (Sec. 1, domain adaptation).
up to 11.55 F1 improvement on ACL-ARC (Sec. 1).
an improvement up to 4 F1 scores in LINNAEUS NER dataset (Sec. 1, knowledge update).
limits: Limitations section was not recovered from the packet or targeted reads.
evidence_quote: We replace FFN in PLM with a Differentiable Plug-in key-value Memory (DPM)

title: LQ-LoRA: Low-rank Plus Quantized Matrix Decomposition for Efficient Language Model Finetuning
question: Can a pretrained matrix be factored into a fixed quantized component plus a trainable low-rank component, so that memory-efficient finetuning starts from a better initialization than zero?
mechanism: Each pretrained W is decomposed as W ~ Q + L1 L2 with Q quantized (NormalFloat) and rank r. Alternating steps (Eq. 2): L1, L2 <- SVD(W - Q, r); then Q <- Quantize(W - L1 L2); Q(0) = 0. An integer linear program assigns bit-width and block size per matrix under a global memory budget. A data-aware variant weights the reconstruction by an approximate Fisher information matrix from calibration samples.
training: The decomposition uses no gradient descent (alternating SVD and quantization; ILP for allocation). The data-aware variant uses Fisher statistics from calibration samples. Then only L1 and L2 are finetuned by gradient descent on downstream data (instruction data, or C4 in the compression setting).
setup: RoBERTa; LLaMA-2 7B and 70B. Evaluation: C4 and WikiText-2 perplexity, 5-shot MMLU (Sec. 4).
numbers: 2.75-bit LLaMA-2-70B model (which has 2.85 bits on average when including the low-rank components and requires 27GB of GPU memory) (Abstract).
we are able to compress LLaMA-2-70B to 2.85 bits with only a small perplexity degradation (Intro).
limits: The authors state that zero initialization may not be optimal when quantization error is large (Intro). Limitations beyond that were not recovered; the Sec. 3 text on RPCA convergence guarantees is cut in the packet.
evidence_quote: performing a single step of the iterative algorithm with the initialization Q(0) = Quantize(W).

title: Spectral Adapter: Fine-Tuning in Spectral Space
question: Does tuning the top singular-vector space of a pretrained weight (additively or by rotation) beat LoRA-style low-rank adapters at a fixed trainable-parameter budget?
mechanism: Take the SVD W = U S V^T of each pretrained weight. Spectral AdapterA: [U1 + A_U U2] S [V1 + A_V V2], an additive update to the top-r singular-vector columns with A_U, A_V zero-initialized. Spectral AdapterR: rotate the top-r columns with orthogonal r x r matrices R_U, R_V (identity init, Cayley parameterization). The rest of the factorization merges back into one weight.
training: Gradient fine-tuning of the top-r spectral parameters, after a one-time SVD of each pretrained weight. The SVD cost grows with model size (Sec. 5 limitations).
inference_cost: 'Negligible runtime and storage overhead' for Spectral AdapterA versus LoRA at rank 8 (Sec. 4.4, Fig. 8).
setup: DeBERTaV3-base on GLUE (Table 1); Mistral 7B on GSM8K (Table 2); Llama3 8B on Orca Math with GSM8K evaluation (Fig. 1); a diffusion model.
numbers: All methods except full fine-tuning maintain approximately 0.23% trainable parameters (Fig. 1 caption).
Pre-Trained − 37.91 ± 1.34 (GSM8K, Mistral 7B, Table 2).
limits: Authors state a limitation in the choice of tuning the top spectral space, which is only theoretically verified under simple settings; the SVD cost grows with model size (Sec. 5).
evidence_quote: To ensure zero initialization as often done for PEFT methods, we initialize AU and AV both at zero.

title: RandLoRA: Full-rank parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large models
question: When LoRA underperforms full fine-tuning, is it due to the reduced trainable-parameter count or to the rank deficiency of the update?
mechanism: A set of fixed, non-trainable random low-rank matrices is the basis. The weight update is a learned linear combination of these bases, where the learned combination is a diagonal scaling applied to the fixed random matrices. Only the diagonal scalings are optimized, which the authors say yields full-rank updates with LoRA-level memory.
training: Gradient training of the diagonal scaling coefficients, with the random bases held fixed. Trained on vision (DinoV2, CLIP over 21 image datasets) and LLaMA3-8B on eight commonsense tasks (Fig. 1 caption).
setup: DinoV2, CLIP (21 image datasets), LLaMA3-8B on 8 commonsense reasoning tasks; Qwen2-0.5b and Phi3-3b in Table 1.
numbers: Table 1 (average over 8 commonsense tasks), Phi3-3b at 170k trainable parameters: 65.4 82.3 81.4 84.6 85.0 84.7 85.2. Column headers are garbled in the extracted text, so the mapping of these values to methods was not recovered.
limits: Limitations section was not recovered from the packet or targeted reads.
evidence_quote: By solely learning scaling coefficients for the linear combination of the random low-rank bases

title: Efficient Knowledge Feeding to Language Models: A Novel Integrated Encoder-Decoder Architecture
question: Can in-context vectors built from latent embeddings replace in-prompt demonstrations and improve question answering over RAG and fine-tuned baselines?
mechanism: Interp: demonstrations are encoded with the LLM's latent embeddings into one in-context vector (ICV). The vector is added to the LLM's latent states at inference, so demonstrations are not placed in the prompt. The architecture pairs an encoder-decoder with cross-attention; the exact formula for building and applying the ICV was not recovered from the packet or targeted reads.
training: Not recovered. The ICV model is described as about 140M parameters, and the fine-tuned BART baseline is fine-tuned on each dataset.
inference_cost: Not quantified in the parts read; the abstract claims reduced computational cost and memory qualitatively.
setup: NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA (exact match, Table 1); RAG baselines with BGE retrievers and Phi-3, LLaMA, Gemma readers.
numbers: ICV Model 0.61 0.67 0.72 against Fine-Tuned BART 0.62 0.70 0.68 (NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA exact match, Table 1).
RAG (BGE + Gemma) 0.60 0.73 0.71 (Table 1).
limits: The ICV model is below fine-tuned BART on NQ (0.61 vs 0.62) in Table 1. Other limitations were not recovered.
evidence_quote: used to shift the latent states of the LLM, enhancing the generation
novelty_note: Converts demonstrations into a latent vector that shifts the LLM's activations at inference, instead of a prompt. The paper does not edit weights.

title: MemInsight: Autonomous Memory Augmentation for LLM Agents
question: Can an LLM agent's memory be structured by autonomously generated attributes so that retrieval of past interactions is more accurate?
mechanism: A backbone LLM extracts attribute-value pairs A = F_LLM(D) = {(a_j, v_j)} from each interaction, at entity or conversation level and turn or session granularity. These annotate the memory entry, and the attribute embeddings are averaged for cosine-similarity retrieval (Appendix B, D.1).
training: None indicated: attribute mining is by prompting the backbone LLM (Table 8 prompts).
numbers: outperforms a RAG baseline by 34% in recall for LoCoMo retrieval (Abstract).
boosts persuasiveness of recommendations by up to 14% (Abstract, LLM-REDIAL).
limits: Limitations were not recovered from the packet.

title: Tracr-Injection: Distilling Algorithms into Pre-trained Language Models
question: Can an algorithm compiled with tracr be distilled into a pretrained LM's residual stream as a linearly decodable subspace, improving out-of-distribution behaviour?
mechanism: Compile a RASP algorithm with tracr (causal=True) to get a target transformer. Fine-tune pretrained GPT-2-large with L = alpha L_CE + beta L_ALG + gamma L_KL. L_ALG = (1/k) sum_i (1 - cos(h_i^mapped, h_i^compiled)) aligns a linear projection of the pretrained residual stream to the compiled model's residual stream across layers. The final residual stream is projected onto the learned subspace and the orthogonal component is replaced (intervention, cut in packet).
training: Gradient fine-tuning of GPT-2-large on the algorithm task data with cross-entropy, the cosine alignment loss, and KL loss on Fineweb text. Data sizes not recovered.
setup: GPT-2-large; Shuffle-Dyck recognition, counting characters, adding two numbers; GLUE SST-2 and MRPC for out-of-distribution tests (Table 2 and App. D).
numbers: set α = β = γ = 1 (Sec. 3, loss weights).
Finetuning + KL 100.0% 569.3; Tracr Injection 99.9% 569.9 (text fragment; column labels not recovered from extraction).
limits: Authors report that the method does not fully generalize out-of-distribution; they propose future work on distilling causal structure (Sec. 5).
evidence_quote: our method creates an interpretable subspace within the model’s residual stream, which can be decoded into the variables present in the code of the RASP algorithm.

title: SingLoRA: Low Rank Adaptation Using a Single Matrix
question: Does learning a single low-rank matrix and using its transpose, rather than LoRA's two matrices, give more stable training at fewer parameters?
mechanism: Replace LoRA's B A with a single matrix A in R^{n x r} so the update is A A^T (Eq. 2). The symmetric form removes inter-matrix scale conflicts, and the paper gives an infinite-width analysis of stable feature learning. Extension to non-square matrices is described in Sec. 4.
training: Gradient training of A (learning-rate sweeps; Dreambooth finetuning uses 400 iterations and LR 1e-3 per Sec. 6.2). Data: MNLI for LLaMA-7B, GLUE for RoBERTa and GPT-2, DreamBooth for Stable Diffusion.
inference_cost: Matched to LoRA in principle; counted as negligible in the text, not quantified in the parts read.
setup: RoBERTa and GPT-2 on GLUE (Table 1); LLaMA-7B on MNLI (Table 2, Fig. 2); Stable Diffusion on DreamBooth (Table 3).
numbers: DINO similarity score of 0.151, compared to scores of 0.148 and 0.143 for DoRA and LoRA (Abstract).
LoRA exhibits a larger variation of up to 4.8% (Sec. 6.3, LR sweep on MNLI).
limits: Authors list combination with DoRA as a future direction (Sec. 7). Other limitations were not recovered.
evidence_quote: This simple design inherently removes inter-matrix scale conflicts, ensuring stable optimization, and roughly halves the parameter count.

title: Multiple Choice Learning of Low-Rank Adapters for Language Modeling
question: Can K LoRA adapters trained with a winner-takes-all (multiple choice learning) loss make a language model produce diverse, plausible continuations at inference?
mechanism: K LoRA adapters share a frozen backbone. For each (c, x), compute log p(x|c; theta_k) for each k and select k* = argmax_k. The WTA loss L_WTA = -E[max_k log p(x|c; theta_k)] updates only the winning adapter with a full gradient; the others get weaker gradients (Fig. 1). A temperature tau is introduced in the method (details cut in packet). At inference each adapter gives one hypothesis.
training: Gradient training of K LoRA adapters with the WTA loss, with epsilon = 0.05 and r = 8 in the K sweep (Table 1). Data: AudioCaps, Clotho (audio captioning), TextCaps (vision), and machine translation.
inference_cost: Authors claim the method 'natively generates diverse and plausible sequences in a single forward pass'. Cost per hypothesis or in K is not quantified in the parts read.
setup: Audio captioning (AudioCaps, Clotho), visual captioning (TextCaps), machine translation; Qwen2-Audio is cited as the scale example for the lm_head size.
numbers: LoRA-MLE (r = 8) 1 2.203 2.812 (Table 1, K=1; AudioCaps, Clotho test loss).
LoRA-MLE (r = 8 × 5) 1 2.181 2.910 (Table 1, the 5-adapter baseline row).
limits: Authors note the WTA training can collapse, with the same adapter winning every time, and that K separate models increase training and memory cost (Sec. 3.2). The LoRA-MCL rows of Table 1 were not recovered from extraction.
evidence_quote: Gradients (purple arrows) are stronger for the winning hypothesis (k⋆ ).

title: FIM-LoRA: Task-Informative Rank Allocation for LoRA via Calibration-Time Gradient-Variance Estimation
question: Can per-layer LoRA rank be allocated before fine-tuning from gradient-variance (empirical Fisher diagonal) estimates on the LoRA-B matrices, at no extra cost in the final adapter?
mechanism: Run T = 8 calibration mini-batches. F_ii = (1/T) sum_t (dL_t/dtheta_i)^2 is the empirical Fisher diagonal on each LoRA-B matrix. The layer score s_l is the mean of that matrix (Eq. 4). Algorithm 1 allocates integer ranks under budget B = r L by water-filling with a ceiling and a floor r_min. Adapters are then resized in place, keeping the leading rows of A.
training: Eight backward passes on calibration batches before fine-tuning, then standard LoRA gradient training. GLUE (DeBERTa-v3-base) and commonsense reasoning (LLaMA-3-8B).
inference_cost: Eight calibration backward passes; the paper states no change in serving or training overhead and a ~256x memory saving over full-model Fisher estimation for r = 16, d_in = 4096.
setup: DeBERTa-v3-base on GLUE (Table 1); LLaMA-3-8B on seven commonsense tasks (Table 3); MNLI calibration batch sweep (Table 5).
numbers: FIM-LoRA matches LoRA (88.6 vs. 88.7) at the same parameter budget (Abstract).
LoRA 68.74 Avg; FIM-LoRA (rmin = 8) 68.47 Avg (Table 3, LLaMA-3-8B commonsense).
8 67.01 67.74 68.47 (Table 4, 8 calibration batches; r_min = 1, 4, 8).
limits: The authors report that at r_min = 1 the method costs about 1.7 accuracy points on commonsense; at typical budgets (r = 8-16), 'accuracy gains over uniform LoRA are below seed noise'. Only LLaMA-3-8B is tested for decoders.
evidence_quote: At typical budgets (r = 8–16), accuracy gains over uniform LoRA are below seed noise.

title: MemToolAgent: Leveraging Memory for Tool Using Agents Based on Environment and User Feedback
question: Can an agent improve tool use by retrieving past user-agent experiences, with a dynamically chosen number of entries and reflections from failures, without fine-tuning the LLM?
mechanism: Memory entries m = (q, a, f, r): the query, the executed tool-call sequence, binary user feedback f, and an LLM-written reflection r when f = 0. At query time, cosine similarities to stored queries are computed, and the number n of entries is set by derivative-based peak detection on the similarity curve (Dynamic n, Alg. 1, with radius, peak number and prominence parameters). The n retrieved entries are placed in the system prompt as in-context examples (Fig. 10).
training: None to the LLM: the paper says the method works without LLM fine-tuning. Memory extraction uses LLM prompting for reflections.
inference_cost: Token counts are reported in Table 5 (input and output tokens); not recovered from the read text.
setup: WorkBench, NESTFUL, PEToolBench; baselines A-MEM and Mem0.
numbers: 29%, 80%, and 17% relative improvements compared to strong baselines on the WorkBench, NESTFUL, and PEToolBench benchmarks, respectively (Abstract).
A-MEM 0.700 0.820; Mem0 0.700 0.820; MemToolAgent 0.820 0.820 (Table 2, PEToolBench tool accuracy, parameter accuracy).
limits: Limitations were not recovered from the packet or targeted reads.
evidence_quote: derivative estimate rather than raw similarity values results in a more robust approach than
novelty_note: Retrieves past tool-call traces and failure reflections into the prompt to change which tools are called and how. This is in-context memory retrieval, not activation steering.

title: LAARA: Layer-Aware Adaptive Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
question: Is uniform LoRA rank provably suboptimal across layers, and can per-layer ranks be allocated search-free from Fisher estimates computed during training?
mechanism: Per-layer score from a lightweight diagonal Fisher estimate: squared gradient norms recorded during standard LoRA training serve as a proxy. Scores are projection-wise normalized, log-compressed, and combined in a blended lora_A/lora_B importance (Eq. 16), with a vote-to-change dampener against rank oscillation. Lemma 1: optimal rank r*_l >= c(eps) erank(F_l), where erank(F) = exp(entropy of normalized eigenvalues) (Eq. 3).
training: Gradient training with Fisher diagonal estimates taken from the training gradients; no separate search or auxiliary objective. GLUE and MathInstruct benchmarks.
inference_cost: Not quantified in the parts read; the method is presented as search-free.
setup: DeBERTa-v3 on GLUE (CoLA, STS-B, RTE, etc.; Table 1, Table 2); MathInstruct (Table 3); r = 64 comparison (Table 4).
numbers: LAARA (Ours) 987,042 68.88 91.91 88.09 against LoRA 1,034,498 68.00 91.62 84.48 (Table 1: parameters, CoLA MCC, STS-B Pearson, RTE acc).
Layer 11 accumulates a Fisher trace nearly two orders of magnitude larger than Layers 0 and 6, confirming (Sec. 1, Observation 2).
limits: Limitations were not recovered from the packet or targeted reads.
evidence_quote: Lemma 1 establishes that layers with higher effective Fisher rank require higher-rank
novelty_note: Predicts a layer's required adapter rank from the effective rank of its Fisher matrix (Lemma 1, Eq. 3), which is a capacity estimate. It does not predict interference between patches.

title: Learning from Failures: Heterogeneous Graph Memory for Small Language Model Tool-Using Agents
question: Can a failure-aware heterogeneous graph memory, plus a precondition gate on risky actions, make a frozen small language model's tool use more reliable?
mechanism: Successful and failed trajectories become a typed heterogeneous graph over tasks, tools, actions, observations, errors, repairs and execution conditions. A trained HG-Retriever ranks a candidate subgraph for a new task. Retrieved evidence is compressed into guidance (what to perform, avoid, check or repair). A policy and precondition gate checks write actions against live observations and graph-derived constraints before execution, and the base LLM stays frozen.
training: A trained heterogeneous graph retriever (gradient training; data not recovered). The base LLM is not trained.
inference_cost: Guidance is compact (paper claim). Prompt-token counts are reported in the results table; not recovered.
setup: tau-bench (Airline and Retail) and AppWorld; executors include Gemma4-26B-A4B and two others (Table 1).
limits: Limitations were not recovered from the packet or targeted reads.
evidence_quote: A policy and precondition gate validates risky actions before execution.
novelty_note: Gate and graph guidance steer which tool actions are taken (allowed, revised or checked before a write). The gate reads live observations and graph constraints, not hidden states, so it is not an activation gate.
